posts.title: Props that ignore the existing structure, platforms with no design: the control gap is still process
posts.excerpt: CROSS Report 1539 and recent HSE prosecutions show the same pattern: temporary works items treated in isolation, existing structure capacity left unchecked, and verbal instructions used in place of calculated safe loads and competent oversight. Under BS 5975-1:2024 the Temporary Works Coordinator must own the full load path and the live register — not just the prop or the platform.
posts.linkedinReady:
Temporary works failures are rarely a single design error. More often they are a process gap.

CROSS Safety Report 1539 (May 2026) is a clear example. Heavy-duty props were proposed to support beams and slab while a defective RC column was removed from the base of a multi-storey block of flats. The props themselves could take the force. The existing beams and slabs could not. No evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up works showed the beams and slab would fail in bending and shear under the redistributed loads. A more complex temporary works system had to be designed before the column could safely be replaced. Without that intervention, a significant part of the building was at risk of collapse.

The same pattern appears in HSE outcomes. At Paxton House (prosecution published June 2026) temporary timber platforms collecting concrete debris had no design and no calculated safe load. An inspection form was completed, but not by a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Workers had a verbal instruction not to overload the platforms — with no safe load established and no effective monitoring. A drilling operative sustained life-changing injuries when the platform collapsed on top of him.

Industry commentary on recent HSE cases reaches the same conclusion: the root cause is frequently missing process, not exotic engineering. No Temporary Works Coordinator formally appointed and active; no live register; no written procedure that is actually followed; supervision assumed rather than documented.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators this week:
• When temporary supports transfer load into existing structure, the design brief must require verification of the full load path — beams, slabs, walls, foundations — not just the capacity of the prop or proprietary unit.
• Reject drawings issued “for approval” that caveats the existing structure without demonstrating it has been assessed.
• Treat crash decks, debris platforms and any temporary boarding that carries load as structures on the Temporary Works Register. “Don’t overload it” is not a design.
• Confirm the person signing inspections is competent for the item and that the Temporary Works Coordinator has closed the permit-to-load / hold point before use.
• Keep the Temporary Works Register current. A folder that is never opened, or a register that stops at tender, does not satisfy BS 5975-1:2024 or CDM duties to plan, manage and monitor.

body.h: CROSS 1539 — props that never checked the existing structure
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1539 (published 14 May 2026) records a near-miss on a multi-storey block of flats. A defective reinforced concrete column at the base was to be replaced with a new steel column. Estimated characteristic load exceeded 1,165 kN; design load around 1,590 kN. Heavy-duty props had already been installed to support beams and slab either side of the column. The prop drawing was status “For Approval” and included a note placing responsibility on the client to confirm the existing structure could safely support additional loads. No evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up works showed the beams and slabs were insufficient to transfer the loads and would fail in bending and shear. The reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and method statement. Without those additional works, removal of the column would have placed a significant part of the building at risk of collapse. The Expert Panel noted a failure of the temporary works procedure: no Temporary Works Coordinator or checking engineer appointed on a significant structure, and design of individual elements in isolation without verifying the full load path.

body.h: Paxton House — temporary platform, no design, life-changing injury
body.p: On 23 February 2024, during refurbishment at Paxton House in the City of London, openings were being cut through concrete floors to form a service riser. Temporary timber platforms had been built under the openings to collect concrete cores and debris. A platform loaded with debris collapsed onto a drilling operative working below. He sustained fractures to his neck and back and a bleed on the brain; he has not been able to return to work. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe loading level. An inspection form had been completed, but not by a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Workers had a verbal instruction to clear platforms and not overload them, with no safe load established and no effective monitoring. Coordination and supervision of who worked where were weak. At Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 11 June 2026, Roots Contractors Ltd (principal contractor) was fined £19,333 plus costs for breaching CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2). Diacutt Ltd was fined £13,000 plus costs for breaching Regulation 15(2). HSE published the outcome on 15 June 2026.

Commentary on recent HSE prosecutions has observed that the root cause is often not a novel technical risk but a missing process. Temporary works that were never planned, coordinated or supervised in the way BS 5975 and CDM 2015 require. No Temporary Works Coordinator formally appointed and actively managing the process; no written temporary works procedure that is actually used; no live register tracking what is designed, checked, permitted and in use; supervision assumed rather than documented. The same sequence appears across platforms, propping into existing structure, sequence changes and access arrangements: the item is treated as “just temporary”; loading is assumed rather than calculated; inspection is a tick rather than a competent review; and coordination remains verbal.

body.h: What a competent contractor and TWC should check this week
ul: When temporary supports transfer load into existing structure, require the design brief to demand verification of the full load path — beams, slabs, walls and foundations — not only the capacity of the prop or proprietary unit.
Reject temporary works drawings that caveat the existing structure without demonstrating that capacity has been assessed and, where necessary, strengthened.

Place crash decks, debris platforms and any temporary boarding that carries people or materials on the Temporary Works Register with a design (or justified standard solution), check category, posted capacity where relevant, and closed permit-to-use.
Confirm that the person completing inspections is competent for the specific item and that the Temporary Works Coordinator has closed the relevant hold point before load or use.

Keep the Temporary Works Register current as works progress. A register that is started at tender and never updated, or that lives only in a folder, does not meet the management requirements of BS 5975-1:2024 or CDM duties to plan, manage and monitor construction work.
Ensure the Temporary Works Coordinator has authority and information to stop work when the temporary condition or load path changes.
